_comment: Per-language security tools `sv` can run, described here rather than in Rust, so adding one is a data change. Three rules shape every entry. First, SARIF only: each tool is asked for SARIF 2.1.0 and nothing else, because one output parser that is trusted is worth more than five that are nearly right, and a tool that cannot emit SARIF is simply not listed yet. Second, a tool that is not installed reports NOT RUN and how to install it — never a clean pass, which is the whole reason this file exists rather than a shell script. Third, `rules` maps the tool's own rule ids to requirements one at a time, and each entry says in `what` what the rule detects. The `what` is not decoration: `crates/sv-check/tests/citations.rs` compares it with the text of every requirement it cites and fails when they share no vocabulary. Every citation in this file was wrong before that guard existed — `V1.2.1` is output encoding and was cited for SQL injection by seven rules — because nothing read the requirement back. A blanket list per tool would credit bandit's SQL rule with everything bandit knows about; a finding whose rule id is not in the map carries no requirement at all, which is a fair thing to be and is shown as such.

adapters.name: Bandit
adapters.note: Bandit has no SARIF formatter of its own; `bandit-sarif-formatter` registers one, which is why the install line names two packages. Bandit installed without it exits with `invalid choice: 'sarif'` and writes nothing, which is reported as not run with that message attached rather than as a clean scan. Bandit also exits non-zero when it finds something, which is not a failure to run: only a missing report counts as that.

adapters.name: Brakeman
adapters.note: Brakeman only understands Rails applications. On a Ruby app that is not Rails it exits without a report, which is recorded as not run rather than as nothing found. Rule ids are Brakeman's warning codes, BRAKE plus the code in four digits, taken from lib/brakeman/warning_codes.rb in Brakeman 8.0.6 and checked on 25 September 2026 against a real SARIF run over crates/sv-check/tests/fixtures/brakeman/app, whose output is kept beside it; fifteen of the ids here appeared in that run. The ids written before that check were mostly wrong: BRAKE0002 is cross-site scripting and was mapped as SQL, BRAKE0013 is eval and was mapped as OS command injection, BRAKE0016 is file access and was mapped as SQL, BRAKE0102 is a 2016 Rails CVE and was mapped as a secret in the source, and BRAKE0000, the SQL injection code itself, was not mapped at all. Codes for individual Rails CVEs are not mapped. An id that is not mapped shows as a finding carrying no requirement rather than as a wrong one.

adapters.name: Semgrep
adapters.note: The only entry that reads more than one language, and the only one that fetches its rules from the network the first time it runs. `sv` itself opens no connection; this tool does, which is why it is listed with that said rather than left to be discovered.
